title: #bobbycannavale #jamescorden #neilpatrickharris #theatrereview #theat...
transcript: Some plays are brilliant and captivating in their own right, while others rely heavily on good actors with genuine chemistry. I would argue that Art is an example of the latter, and that the new production on Broadway proves it. Bobby Cannavale, James Corden and Neil Patrick Harris play three longtime friends who first clash over a completely white painting, and later clash over just about everything else too. The premise is intriguing but loses its novelty pretty quickly, and I found myself really nervous about 15 minutes in that it wasn't gonna go anywhere. Thankfully, once we got into the meat of the piece and had all three guys on stage together, that's where things really started to pick up. I felt that the out-of-place, fourth-wall-breaking monologues and even some of the duo scenes just couldn't hold a flame to the energy and momentum brought by their chemistry as a trio. I thought all three actors were decent, but James Corden is the one who stole the show, admittedly to my surprise. He had a lot of the funniest material and embodied his character the most effortlessly. I actually think that more than half of my laughter throughout my viewing can be attributed to him. With all that said, I think I'm going to remember the experience of the play as opposed to anything about the actual play, if that makes sense. And there's nothing inherently wrong with that, but it's just to say that this is a piece that only requires a surface level of engagement. In fact, sometimes that's just what the doctor ordered. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
reasoning: The reviewer finds the play itself underwhelming ('loses its novelty pretty quickly,' 'only requires a surface level of engagement') but appreciates the actors' chemistry, especially James Corden. He acknowledges enjoyment but frames it as a lightweight experience he won't deeply remember, landing squarely in mixed territory.
